source_text: Et haec quidem de patre et de filio et de spiritu sancto breuiter sint nobis dicta, et strictim posita, et non longa disputatione porrecta. latius enim potuerunt porrigi, et propensiore disputatione produci, quandoquidem ad testimonium, quod ita se habeat fides uera, totum et uetus et nouum testamentum possit adduci. sed quia obluctantes aduersus ueritatem semper haeretici sincerae traditionis et catholicae fidei controuersiam solent trahere, scandalizati in Christum, quod etiam deus et per scripturas asseratur et a nobis hoc esse credatur, merito a nobis (ut omnis a fide nostra auferri possit haeretica calumnia) de eo quod et deus sit Christus sic est disputandum, ut non impediat scripturae ueritatem, sed nec nostram fidem, qua unus deus et per scripturas promitur, et a nobis tenetur et creditur. tam enim illi qui Iesum Christum ipsum deum patrem dicunt, quam etiam illi qui hominem illum tantummodo esse uoluerunt, erroris sui et peruersitatis origines et causas inde rapuerunt, quia cum animaduerterent scriptum esse quod unus sit deus, non aliter putauerunt istam tenere se posse sententiam, nisi aut hominem tantum Christum, aut certe deum patrem putarent esse credendum. sic enim calumnias suas colligere consueuerunt, ut errorem proprium approbare nitantur. et quidem illi qui Iesum Christum patrem dicunt, ista praetendunt: si unus deus, Christus autem deus, pater est Christus, quia unus deus: si non pater sit Christus, dum et deus filius Christus, duo dii contra scripturas introducti esse uideantur. qui autem hominem tantummodo Christum esse contendunt, ex diuerso sic colligunt: si alter pater, alter est filius, pater autem deus, et Christus deus, non ergo unus deus, sed duo dii introducuntur pariter, pater et filius; ac si unus deus, consequenter homo Christus, ut merito pater sit deus unus. re uera quasi inter duos latrones cruci figitur dominus, quo modo fixus aliquando est: et ita excipit haereticorum istorum ex utroque latere sacrilega conuicia. Sed neque scripturae sanctae, neque nos causas illis perditionis et caecitatis afferimus, si qua in medio diuinarum ro litterarum euidenter posita aut uidere nolunt, aut uidere non possunt. nos enim et scimus et legimus et credimus et tenemus unum esse deum, qui fecit caelum pariter ac terram, quoniam nec alterum nouimus aut nosse (cum nullus sit) aliquando poterimus. ego sum, inquit, deus: e non est praeter me iustus et saluans. et alio in loco: ego primus et nouissimus, et praeter me non est deus. quis sicut ego? et: quis mensus est palmo caelum, et terram pugillo? quis suspendit montes in pondere, et nemora in statera? et Ezechias: ut sciant omnes quia tu es deus solus. ipse praeterea dominus: quid me interrogas de bono? unus deus bonus. apostolus quoque Paulus: guz solus, inquit, habet immortalitatem, et lucem habitat inaccessibilem; quem uidit hominum nemo, nec uidere potest. et alio in loco: mediator autem unius non est; deus autem unus est. sed quo modo hoc tenemus et legimus et credimus, sic scripturarum caelestium nullam partem praeterire debemus: quippe cum etiam illa quae in scripturis sunt posita Christi diuinitatis insignia nullo modo debemus recusare, ne scripturarum auctoritatem corrumpendo integritatem fidei sanctae corrupisse teneamur. et hoc ergo credamus, siquidem fidelissimum, dei filium Iesum Christum dominum et deum nostrum: quoniam zz principio erat uerbum, et uerbum erat apud deum, et deus erat uerbum. hoc erat in principio apud deum. et uerbum caro factum est, et habitauit in nobis. et: dominus meus et deus meus. et: quorum patres, et ex quibus Christus secundum carnem, qui est super omnia deus benedictus in saecula. Quid ergo dicemus? numquid duos deos scriptura proponit? quomodo ergo dicit, quia deus unus est? aut numquid non et Christus deus est? quomodo ergo, dominus meus et deus meus, Christo dictum est? totum igitur hoc nisi cum propria ueneratione et legitima disputatione teneamus, merito scandalum haereticis praebuisse credemur, non utique ex scripturarum caelestium uitio, quae numquam fallunt, sed humani erroris praesumptione, qua haeretici esse uoluerunt. et in primis illud retorquendum in istos qui duorum nobis deorum controuersiam facere praesumunt. scriptum est, quod negare non possunt, quoniam unus est dominus. de Christo ergo quid sentiunt? dominum esse, aut illum omnino non esse? sed dominum illum omnino non dubitant: ergo si uera est illorum ratiocinatio, iam duo sunt domini.. quomodo igitur iam secundum scripturas unus est dominus? et magister unus Christus est dictus; attamen legimus, quod magister sit etiam apostolus Paulus. non ergo iam unus magister: duos enim magistros secundum ista colligimus. quomodo igitur secundum scripturas unus magister Christus? unus in scripturis bonus dictus est deus; sed iisdem in scripturis bonus etiam Christus positus est. non igitur, si recte colligunt, unus bonus, sed etiam duo boni. quomodo igitur secundum scripturarum fidem unus bonus esse refertur? ac si non putant aliqua ratione offici posse ei quod unus dominus est, per illud quod est dominus et Christus; neque ei quod unus est magister, per illud quod est magister et Paulus; aut illi quod unus est bonus, per illud quod bonus sit nuncupatus et Christus; eadem ratione intellegant offici non posse ab illo quod unus est deus, ei quod deus pronuntiatus est et Christus.
pass_a_gloss: We have briefly stated these things about the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, and have set them forth succinctly, and have not extended them in a long discussion. For they could have been extended more broadly, and produced with a more detailed discussion, since the entire Old and New Testament can be adduced as testimony that the true faith is such. But because heretics, who are always opposed to the truth, are accustomed to draw out a controversy against the sincere tradition and the Catholic faith, being scandalized by Christ, because He is also God, as is asserted by the Scriptures and believed by us, it is right that we should discuss the fact that Christ is God in such a way that it does not hinder the truth of Scripture, nor our own faith, by which one God is promised and is believed by us through the Scriptures. For both those who say that Jesus Christ is the Father Himself, and those who want Him to be only a man, have taken the origins and causes of their error from the fact that, when they noticed that it is written that there is one God, they did not think that they could hold this opinion in any other way than by either considering Christ to be only a man, or certainly believing Him to be the Father. Thus, they are accustomed to collect their calumnies in such a way that they strive to approve their own error. And indeed, those who say that Jesus Christ is the Father, put forward this argument: if there is one God, and Christ is God, then Christ is the Father, because there is one God; if Christ is not the Father, then, since He is the Son of God, two Gods are introduced, contrary to Scripture. But those who contend that Christ is only a man, collect their arguments in the opposite way: if the Father is one and the Son is another, and the Father is God, and Christ is God, then two Gods are introduced, the Father and the Son; and if there is one God, then consequently Christ is a man, so that the Father may be the one God. In reality, the Lord is crucified between two thieves, as He was once fixed to the cross, and thus He receives the sacrilegious insults of these heretics from both sides. But we do not bring forth the causes of their perdition and blindness, either from the Holy Scriptures or from ourselves, if they do not want to see, or cannot see, the things that are clearly set forth in the midst of the divine letters. For we know, and read, and believe, and hold that there is one God, who made heaven and earth, since we do not know, nor can we ever know, any other. For it is written: I am God, and there is no one just and saving besides Me. And in another place: I am the first and the last, and there is no God besides Me. Who is like Me? And: Who has measured the heaven with a span, and the earth with a fist? Who has suspended the mountains in a balance, and the forests in a scale? And Ezechias: so that all may know that You are the only God. The Lord Himself also says: Why do you ask Me about what is good? There is one good God. The Apostle Paul also says: He alone has immortality, and He dwells in inaccessible light, whom no man has seen, nor can see. And in another place: A mediator of one is not; but God is one. But just as we hold, and read, and believe this, so we should not pass over any part of the celestial Scriptures; for we should not refuse the signs of Christ's divinity that are set forth in the Scriptures, lest we be held to have corrupted the integrity of the holy faith by corrupting the authority of the Scriptures. And therefore, we should believe that Jesus Christ, the Son of God, is our Lord and God; for it is written: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. This was in the beginning with God. And the Word became flesh, and dwelled among us. And: My Lord and my God. And: Whose fathers were, and from whom Christ was born according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever. What then shall we say? Does Scripture propose two Gods? How then does it say that there is one God? Or does it not also say that Christ is God? How then was it said to Christ: My Lord and my God? Therefore, unless we hold all this with proper veneration and legitimate discussion, we will be believed to have rightly given scandal to the heretics, not because of any fault in the celestial Scriptures, which never fail, but because of the presumption of human error, by which the heretics have wanted to be. And first of all, we should retort to those who presume to make a controversy about two Gods: it is written, which they cannot deny, that there is one Lord. What then do they think about Christ? Is He the Lord, or is He not the Lord at all? But they do not doubt that He is the Lord; therefore, if their reasoning is true, then there are already two Lords. How then is there one Lord according to the Scriptures? And it is said that there is one Master, Christ; yet we read that the Apostle Paul is also a master. Therefore, there is not one Master; for we gather from these things that there are two masters. How then is there one Master, Christ, according to the Scriptures? One God is said to be good in the Scriptures; but in the same Scriptures, Christ is also said to be good. Therefore, if they reason correctly, there is not one good God, but two goods. How then is there one good God according to the faith of the Scriptures? And if they do not think that some office can be attributed to the fact that there is one Lord, through the fact that Christ is Lord; nor to the fact that there is one Master, through the fact that Paul is a master; or to the fact that there is one good God, through the fact that Christ is called good; then they should understand by the same reasoning that some office cannot be attributed to the fact that there is one God, through the fact that Christ is called God.
